utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Case number IT-04-74-PT, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask for appearances, starting with the Prosecution. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecutor herself, Carla Del Ponte, together with Ken Scott and Daryl Mundis. We also have a case manager - I don't know how you say this in French - Skye Winner, and counsel Josee D'Aoust. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Prosecutor. I'm now turning to Defence counsel, starting with Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'm Michael Karnavas for Dr. Prlic. With me is Suzana Tomanovic, co-counsel, and Ana Vlahovic, our case manager and legal assistant as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Bozidar Kovacic for Mr. Slobodan Praljak as the lead counsel, and let me introduce my co-counsel, Ms. Nika Pinter, so we are shortening time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [Interpretation] ... the Trial Chamber and the president, I hope that I will be allowed to withdraw from this case immediately, without any prior approval of my counsel [as interpreted]. I hope that we will be able to discuss this today in a public session so that I can give you reasons for this request of mine. Due to an omission of the Registry, a number of documents were delivered to all parties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... this is a question we will tackle later. For the time being, we are just going with appearances. Next counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next to me is legal counsel Ms. Krystyna Grinberg and case manager, Ms. Ida Jurkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Appearing on behalf of Mr. Pusic, we have here Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, Roger Sahota, and Nermin Mulalic, case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very shortly I'll have the opportunity to ask the accused to introduce themselves because, apart from Mr. Praljak, I do not know the other accused. I have never seen them before. I shall ask them later on to introduce themselves. Today, as you know, based on Rule 73 bis, we are holding a Pre-Trial Conference. Before moving to the agenda of the Pre-Trial Conference, as you know, as a Pre-Trial Judge, I had invited Madam Prosecutor to appear before the Trial Chamber in order to explain to the Chamber how the Prosecution intended to present its case and in which deadline, which time period they were planning to do so. She was not able to be there at the last Pre-Trial or Status Conference because she had other commitments, as they were celebrating the 60th anniversary of the ICJ and Madam Prosecutor had told me that she was going to set forth her position at the Pre-Trial Conference. By way of a reminder, I shall summarise the problem, also for the accused. As you know, the Prosecution presented to the Trial Chamber, to the Defence counsel, and to the accused, its pre-trial brief. There was a reply by the Defence counsel, and the Prosecution also forwarded a list of over 400 witnesses and a list of exhibits, some 9.500 exhibits. On this basis, the Trial Chamber tried to ascertain the time period given to the Prosecution for their case. We made this calculation on the basis of the Prosecution documents, and we would have had to have a trial that would have taken three years only for the Prosecution case. In addition to the three years, there would be a reply by the Defence. All the Defence counsels said that, based on the principle of the fair trial, they wanted to have the same time as the Prosecution for their case. As I told you, it's a simple calculation: This would take 21 years, which is absolutely impossible. Why is it impossible? For the following reason: Resulting from Security Council Resolutions, two relevant Resolutions; Resolution 1503 and Resolution 1534. The Security Council invited the Tribunal to take all necessary steps so that trials be concluded by 2008, and at the appeals level, for proceedings to be concluded by 2010. The Security Council decided it had to be seized and remain seized of the issue, and requested from the Prosecutor and from the President of the Tribunal to present a status or progress report as to the completion strategy of our Tribunal for the completion of our work. In this framework, the Prosecutor and the president go to New York every six months to present such reports. This is quite a straight and rigid framework imposed on us by the Security Council. Therefore we can't go beyond the date of 2008. This has a series of consequences as to the presentation of evidence, at the latest Status Conference the Prosecution presented a ten-point plan, which should make it possible, according to the Prosecution, to resolve quite a number of problems. As to the Defence, they agreed on certain points and disagreed on others. Therefore, after hearing Madam Prosecutor and the Defence counsel, the Trial Chamber will issue a decision as to the time allocated to the Prosecution for their case. So first of all, I shall give the floor to Mrs. Carla Del Ponte, who is going to explain to us in which way she and her team are planning to conduct their case. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. Your Honours, Defence counsel. Nobody wants to be here for 20 years, I believe. I'm certain of it. And I also believe that the Security Council gave us some deadlines, some dates that did not change, even if, as you heard it on the -- at the hearing of the 12th of April, President Meron and President Pocar told the Security Council that we will need all of 2009 in order to conclude trials. I believe that this trial can go on until the end of 2009, if it is necessary, but I believe it is possible to conclude this trial within a shorter period of time. I read the transcript of the latest Status Conference with great attention and care because, as you can see, Ken Scott presented our plan in ten points which should make it possible to present our case within a year. I do not intend to present these points again because you're all familiar with them, but allow me, Mr. President, to express a few thoughts which I believe are relevant and may introduce a good discussion. First item: Rule 65 ter (F). Mr. President, you ruled that our application should be denied because it failed to meet the requirements set forth by this rule. In my view, the Defence in their pre-trial brief failed to meet the requirements under this rule. Indeed, Mr. President, you acknowledged it yourself, and I quote: "It can be reasonably required from the Defence that they should do more." So I think that we should require from the Defence that they should do more. Why? Because if they do, we shall be able to change our programme. As to Rule 67(A), there, you said that you should leave it to the Defence when they deem it appropriate, but I'm -- allow me to say this: Since the Trial Chamber required from the Defence that they do say whether they are going to invoke the defence of alibi or any other special defence, if we knew this ourselves, it would make our case, the Prosecution case, easier. Here again, allow me to insist on this point because we think that this will be a great help. It would really help us to reduce the time we need for the Prosecution case. Now, when it comes to cross-examination, it is up to you, Trial Chamber, to you, Mr. President, to make your decision. We have made some calculations. I discussed that with my colleagues only this morning. I think that we can present our case within 450 hours but, of course, I do urge you to apply Rule 73 bis even more, and this is not only for the Defence but also for the Prosecutor. If I put questions during examination-in-chief that you do not deem relevant, please stop us. Stop the Prosecution, stop the Defence, if you feel that we are wasting time, wasting time because this would not be really relevant to the case which is ours. As to adjudicated facts, this is Rule 94, or judicial notice. Remember the motions we filed. 88 adjudicated facts were granted, but we mentioned 515 facts in our motion. And allow me to insist on this, insist on the international armed conflict as an issue. My colleague reminded you of the appeals judgement in Kordic and Cerkez. Soon we are going to have another appeals decision which is likely to affirm the existence of an international armed conflict in Bosnia with the involvement of Croatia. So I shall allow myself to file another motion with new elements in it, and I believe that we would be greatly helped because we can't just call witnesses for each case. We have various witnesses and they are going to speak to the armed conflict but, of course, you've got all the answers to provide you with, and I can assure you, Mr. President, Your Honours, that if we do so, we can really save a lot of time. As to 92 bis and 89(F), just go back to what you said yourself, Mr. President. You said it was denied temporarily. And I like that word, "temporarily," and I think that gradually motions will be filed. I believe you have received this chart, so you have an overview, a better overview of the case, and I must say that with this chart, we'll deal with exhibits more efficiently. I believe there is one major point. It's the dossiers on the crime base. We have 14 files or dossiers because there are 14 crime bases. They are going to be prepared gradually but we do ask the Defence to look into the dossiers and especially to tell us which are going to be the points that they are going to dispute, under Rule 65 ter (F). I think you have to ask the Defence to commit themselves. We are going to do an enormous work. I mean, it's a lot of work to prepare the files and dossiers, but if we do that, the Defence will have exact notice of all the crime bases. We tried to have an estimate of the time we could save thanks to the dossiers. We could save ten to 15 per cent of the overall time we need for the Prosecution case. Other extremely important point: Photocopies. You know that we have an electronic system, the so-called e-court, but actually I notice that everybody likes to have paper in front of them. So, of course, we can access e-court, it can be used, but as a matter of fact, and you in the first place, and I understand you, Mr. President, you want to have a paper file. But there is a problem with that. Who is going to do the photocopying of all the dossiers? Because I have to tell you, as the office of the Prosecutor, I cannot photocopy, make 8, 10 or 12 photocopies -- well, dossiers, or photocopy 8, 10, 12 times each and every document. Look at the instructions delivered by President Meron. Everybody should take care of their own needs. So I do urge you, Mr. President, to make a decision to decide who is going to do what. I can tell you that we are not in a position, not at all in a position, to photocopy everything for everybody. This is not captatio benevolentia, but I can tell you straight, I could do the photocopying for the Judges, for the Trial Chamber, but that's all I can do. So in conclusion, I can confirm that, thanks to our ten point plan, we can present our case, [In English] the Prosecution case, including cross-examining, [Interpretation] to one calendar year, and as Mr. Scott said, [In English] if the Chamber sits 47 weeks, five days a week, with 4.5 hours of testimony per day. [Interpretation] This is our working plan. Allow me to say, Mr. President, that we keep harping on 400 or so witnesses. It is true that we have that many witnesses on our list, but I had a fight with my people at our meeting this morning. I said what are 450 witnesses? I want to know who are the viva voce witnesses, those who are going to come here to The Hague to testify. I can give you a number, a figure. I can tell you how many viva voce witnesses we are going to have. We are going to have 180 viva voce witnesses, and out of them, you're going to have some who can come under the 89 bis (F) Rule so you can receive a transcript which makes the time even shorter for their testimony. I'd like everybody to take note of this. We are going to -- or we have listed 180 witnesses, and we are hoping to cut down on that number as well, but to do so we need the help of the Trial Chamber and we need the help of each and every Defence counsel. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Madam Prosecutor, thank you very much for this information you conveyed to the four judges of the Bench as to your plan, the plan that you're going to implement to present your case within a seemingly reasonable time, namely some 450 hours. You have made a commitment. You are going to call to the stand only 180 viva voce witnesses, and you also pledge that among the 180 witnesses, you might have some under the 89(F) Rule, which is going to make it possible to save a lot of time. The other main track of your battle plan is the dossiers. We'll come back to this later on. In a few minutes I'm going to give the floor to the Defence counsel and they are also going to shed some light on this, following which we will issue a written decision which will be filed with the Registry before we officially commence the trial tomorrow. So without further ado, I'm going to give the floor to the Defence counsel and then, if you so wish, Madam Prosecutor, you can be released because you have other commitments and we have our agenda. So to be fair, I'm just going to follow the order and I'll start with Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, and welcome, Madam Del Ponte. It's a pleasure having your presence here and it was a pleasure listening to how you believe this case, the Prosecution case, can be finished in 450 hours. I think it's a rather monumental task to do that, Herculean, I would say, and in fact an impossibility. Because the 450 hours as they calculate it, that would be based on if you were to accept their ten-point plan. So much of what we heard today is what we've heard in the past. If you look at the number -- I'll start at the end again. One of my habits is to start at the end and move back forwards. 185 viva voce. Some of these witnesses will be here for two or three days, others may be here only for a day, maybe even perhaps a half a day, but just do the math. It's almost impossible to do 185 witnesses where you have six accused, all with different issues, perhaps. Some may not need to cross-examine a witness but some witnesses we will all need to cross-examine. So when you look at that figure, 185, it becomes virtually impossible. Initially, Your Honour, you indicated that this case would take approximately four years. I think that was a rather modest estimation but I think it was a realistic one. I think it could be done probably within three years. I don't think it can be done in two years, not unless the indictment is reformulated and unless the indictment is more precise. You have a clash of two systems here: One, you have an adversarial indictment. Why do I say that? The indictment has every conceivable mode of liability in it, very much as if you will be in the United States. On the other hand, the procedure at the Tribunal is coming closer and closer to the continental system, the Romano-Germanique system, and what Madam Del Ponte is suggesting is that we move even closer to that, and I agree with her, but there lies the problem; you have a Prosecutor who is a party to the proceedings, unlike what you would have in a civil law system. And I think if you had an indictment drafted as if you were in a civil law system, you would not have it in the way it is drafted in this case where every mode of liability in the alternative is in it. That poses a problem to the Defence because we have to make sure that on each and every count, that we anticipate how any potential evidence may be used on any one of those modes of liability. If the Prosecution is so sure, so sure, that all of these individuals are guilty, and if they are so sure that they have all of the evidence for each and every count, then they should choose. Why the alternatives? Your Honour, you indicated way back, several months ago, that you wanted a proofing chart. That proofing chart should have been instituted when this institution came into place, because if that had been the case, then every indictment from the inception of this Tribunal would have forced the Prosecutor to really have their evidence before they proceeded. We do have a proofing chart. It's only a partial one. It's a good -- they started off on the right foot, finally. It's a lot of work, I understand. I'm sure had they known in advance, they would have done it in advance because I think that they are operating in good faith. On the other hand, it's only a partial one. So when Madam Del Ponte says, well, you know, you have to accept more 92 bis statements, well, we need the complete proofing chart for that. So I do agree with her that maybe we could do better, but we need their entire proofing chart, and until we have that and until you have that, you cannot make that decision. Regarding the photocopying, well, I do agree with Madam Del Ponte that it's taxing. If it's taxing to her, and I'm used to saying that they an armada of staff, a fleet, a legion. We only have here four -- five -- four Prosecutors, but behind them there is 20 others. You've got people listening in to the proceedings, as the proceedings are going on where they are e-mailing and they're able to react. The Defence doesn't have these resources. So I'm -- my heart goes out to her that she doesn't have all these resources for copying, but think of the poor Defence. And by my estimation, we are going to be needing about 15 or 16 copies. I'm not suggesting that the Prosecution do our work or that we do their work, but that is a realistic issue that we need to tackle and it will take all of us to do that, but I welcome her concerns because they are our concerns as well. With respect to the dossiers, sometimes -- we saw a model dossier, if you want to call it that. I don't wish to call it that but if we are going to use a term, let's use that one, but let's not confuse that with a dossier that you would get in a civil law system, please. Let's just make sure of that. What we are talking about is a file, a particular individual file that would deal with certain issues. I welcome that. Why didn't we have that from the beginning? That would have been much easier. In fact, Mr. President, is not your proofing chart in and of itself the dossier that you have been asking for? It would have been much easier. We wouldn't have to go through these machinations, we could all look at the proofing chart and then prepare our own dossiers or files. I don't think that's going to help us that much, but nonetheless, as I indicated last time, I'm fully prepared to engage and work with the Prosecution on that. I suspect that there will be times when we will need to supplement what they are providing you and there will be some times when we will disagree what should be in there, in a particular dossier, but I don't have a problem with that. Adjudicated facts. This is -- I don't mean to sound pedestrian, but it's like a broken record. It's over and over again every time they come in here. We've heard this so many times: If you would only accept more adjudicated facts. Of course, I've been asking for them to reduce their indictment. Nobody hears me on that aisle. We could only accept certain adjudicated facts. Others we had to challenge. Again, Mr. President and Your Honours, when you look at the indictment itself, it's not just the counts, it's everything that's in the indictment; in the four corners, from page 1, from the first word, to the very last word of that indictment. Everything that needs to be challenged. If we don't have to challenge it and if it's not necessary, then why is it in there? Why have this historical background if it's not part of the indictment that I have to challenge? Why is it necessary to have it in there? Because we saw this in the Stakic decision recently in the Appeals Chamber's decision, that in essence everything can come in, everything can be used for context purposes, and so we have to worry about what's in it. And if there is something in the historical fact that we disagree with, we have to challenge it. And I don't want to repeat myself, but last time I did indicate that the problem with this Tribunal was that from its inception it was trying to -- part of their mission, I guess they thought, was a historical truth, try to find a historical record, and so the indictments and the procedure was to figure out who started the war, why did the war start, who is responsible for the war, and so on and so forth, rather than try to reduce the indictment to the individuals that they charge. So now, if you look at this indictment, the Republic of Croatia is on trial. That entire government that existed there was on trial. President Tudjman, the late President Tudjman is on trial in absentia. So is Mr. Susak, so is General Bobetko, and so on and so forth. That's what this case is about. And what they are asking us to do is either accept that in order to reduce the time of trying the case -- in other words, accept that these people and this government and in essence everyone who was a member of the HVO, when you look in the joint criminal enterprise, every single person who was involved essentially is being tried. And because of the wideness of the indictment, it causes us to challenge everything. It's not that we are obstreperous or that we want to be here for the next 20 years, but as I indicated last time, Your Honours, I don't have the discretion of drafting the indictment. I've offered to help them reduce it. I have. I don't have the power to confirm the indictment. But I do have the right, as my clients have that right, to be here and to try to protect them. And so I don't think that we can reduce the time of the trial by accepting adjudicated facts. Facts that we believe were not properly ruled upon in the first place because the indictments perhaps were not as wide, you didn't -- you might not have had the joint criminal enterprise, or the lawyers chose a particular tactic in their case where they wanted only to try the charges in the indictment, disregarding the factual background or other matters that were in the indictment, but I believe that my client, because he was invited to be here by force, due to their indictment, he's entitled to challenge everything. And if something in that indictment is not necessary, take it out, strike it out. Excise it. Make it easier for us. But they can't have it both ways; they can't put it in and then say don't worry about it, just accept it because there is a completion strategy. That's their problem, that's New York's problem, it's not my client's problem. His problem is he's fighting for his future. That's his problem, and he wants to make sure he gets a fair trial. And we are not going to get a fair trial by just agreeing to adjudicated facts. Cross-examination. I agree with Madam Del Ponte that we all need to be vigilant to make sure that we only ask questions that are relevant. If something is not relevant, neither the Prosecution nor the Defence should be asking these questions. I'm in total agreement. On the other hand, it's a well-known tactic, and sometimes it's not a tactic but it's an unnecessary need, for the Prosecution to go into certain areas with a particular witness. The question is can I, as a Defence, go into areas outside the scope of the direct? And the answer to that question, in my opinion is yes, if it's relevant. Absolutely. I'm entitled to go outside the scope of the direct if it's relevant to the case itself. So if the Prosecution because for tactical reasons chooses not to go into a particular area, and I need to, I have to. Sometimes a witness may come here and may have information that I might be able to take out from that witness in order to impeach another witness. Now I have a choice. I can confine my cross-examination or I can call that witness to come back here and to give direct evidence. Again, as long as I'm able to say, convincingly, to you that it's relevant, I should be able to go into those areas. One other issue: We talked about this on previous occasions and, Your Honour Mr. President, you mentioned it yourself. Simply because a reference is made to a document, to one or two lines in a document, you and your colleagues will not just look at that one line or two lines. You will look at the entire document, and I dare say even the footnotes to the document. That's what I would do. So what does that mean? The Prosecution can take literally one minute to introduce a particular document or make reference to one line or two lines, but if in that document hidden some place is a trap, something that might be used, something that I need to explain away, that may take 10 or 20 or 30 minutes for me to get to it. That's why some magic formula doesn't work. I go back. If it's relevant, I'm entitled to do it. And I think the only thing that should prevent me or my colleagues is, is it repetitive? And again, because there are six of us, there may be some very fine, some subtle issues that we each may have, and while it may sound like it's repetitive at first blush, it may not necessarily be so. But again, I think all of us are professional, we all want to move along, and I think the Rules are designed in a way to make sure that you, Mr. President and Your Honours, have maximum control in this courtroom. You control the environment. So if any one of us gets out of hand, is going into areas that are not relevant, is repeating themselves, you have the possibility of intervening. You indicated that you wished perhaps to even begin the questioning yourself. As I noted before and I'll say it again, I have no problem with that. If that's the procedure that's adopted, I'm willing to go along with it. I'm still entitled to my cross-examination, of course. Alibi defences, Rule 67(A). Again, you know, I have to -- I have to take a deep breath when I hear this every time. Why? I get a little emotional, I guess, because maybe after all these years, the Prosecution still doesn't get it that we are in an adversarial system. I don't mean to be mean spirited. I know that they would like to know as much as they want about the Defence so they can begin to actually attack the Defence before we even put on our case, but I have to remind Madam Del Ponte that you have the burden of proof, you have to go forward. It's not for me to give you the alibi defence if I'm going to run one at this point in time. I would agree with her and with all of her colleagues that at some point I have to give them notice of a defence, especially alibi, before the defence puts on their case in chief. Why? The whole purpose of giving notice in alibi, Your Honours, is to make sure that they have an opportunity to investigate that alibi. That's all -- that's what it's all about. But for me at this point in time to disclose my defence, my theory of their -- of my case, to them, after they spent eight years investigating, after they drafted the indictment, and they are saying maybe we can speed things up if the Defence would only cooperate and tell us what they plan on doing in their case, again, we are not in the continental system, we are not in -- this is a mixed system, in the procedure-wise but when you look at the substantive system itself, the Prosecution bears the burden of proof. The burden never, ever shifts. I may have a burden of going forward but the burden rests on the Prosecution. They know it, or they should know it, and if not, they should know it by now, or after today, at least. The pre-trial brief. Again, I think we've gone over this. I think if you look at the combination of all the pre-trial briefs, they have enough knowledge and information there that they know exactly what this case is about, they know what our defences are. I can write a hundred-page brief and waste a tree or two and all of your time, or I can put it down in four pages, which is what I did. I think from those four pages, they can glean enough. Am I going to go after each and point out every flaw or every tactic that I intend to use? Of course, not. But again, keep in mind that I don't have that proofing chart. Had I had the proofing chart, maybe they could make a more legitimate argument, but I think that argument doesn't fly, hasn't flown before, and shouldn't fly right now. And I think they have enough. And even if I were to do another pre-trial brief for them and make it maybe 20 or 30 or 40 pages or 200 pages, it's still not going to shorten them. They are still planning on calling 185 witnesses viva voce. So I covered more or less all the points that Madam Del Ponte brought up, including the ten points, as if we were at the Treaty of Versailles, you know. We have Wilson's 12 points in that instance. I don't think those ten points are going to get us anywhere. I think there are some innovative techniques we are willing to adopt, we are willing to work, but at the end of the day unless that indictment is excised, unless, Mr. President, you order, and I'm not sure whether you can order but if you were to at least encourage the Prosecutor to take another look at that indictment and only choose the modes of liability that they could actually prove, that they believe that they could actually prove, as opposed to putting in all the alternatives, I think if they were to do that, you would find that one-third, if not one-half, of that indictment would be thrown out. They would still have the other half. So if you got four years you predicted, you throw out 50 per cent of the indictment, you get to your two years right there. So I've solved the problem. Then we can take on board some of their other solutions. I'm willing to assist them in trying to excise some of those parts of the indictment. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Thank you, Madam Del Ponte.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. I shall now give the floor to Mrs. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Today we have gone over once again all the material covered at the previous Status Conference. The Prosecutor has outlined her ten points and I don't intend to address them once more. I agree for the most part with what my colleague Mr. Karnavas has said. These ten points are such that it is not possible to accept them. Therefore, the plan presented by the Office of the Prosecutor is impossible to carry out. Today, it is Your Honours who have the most difficult task because Your Honours have to reach a decision in this difficult situation and say what the optimum time for the presentation of the Prosecution case is. I think we have to bear in mind that today we have before us a problem of time. I am concerned that this may go against the interests of justice. Your Honours should not forget that we have before us the most complex indictment ever seen at this Tribunal. Never before has there been an indictment for as large a number of accused. It is not only these six men here who are accused but a large number of others as well. Never before has so much evidence been before a Chamber. Never before has all this had to be compressed into a time period of two years. I will be very happy if all this could be over in a year and a half. However, the time, the pressure of time, should by no means be allowed to go against the interests of justice. I fully agree with my colleague Mr. Karnavas when he says that we cannot be expected to assist the Prosecution. However, we can and must be expected to assist the Chamber. We are prepared to do this at every point. I have already stated what I feel about the dossiers. They are of great assistance to the Court because they represent a shortening of the work that was to be done when Your Honours asked that a list of witnesses be presented. We have had an opportunity of seeing a dossier of this kind, and it is of assistance, yes, to Your Honours and to the Defence. However, I'm not sure that it will save time. The ten or 15 per cent of the time that the Prosecution feels might be saved perhaps will be saved by the Prosecution, but the Defence will need that time to prepare, and I feel we have to keep in mind that as of now, the Defence must be given time to prepare for all the evidence it is presented with. The plan we have received for the first witnesses includes evidence we have not yet received. Today, we have to prepare for the witnesses who are to testify next week and we have not yet received all of the materials. Some of the materials are still coming in. Therefore, we must be given enough time to prepare. Finally, let me repeat that the time that the Chamber will set should be realistic and should be the optimum amount of time. The Defence should not be put under pressure to accept the adjudicated facts presented by the Prosecution because it is not up to the Defence to present this case and this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, after my esteemed colleagues Mr. Karnavas and Ms. Nozica presented their arguments in response to what we heard from the Prosecutor, I do not wish to repeat what they have already said. I will therefore draw attention only to three issues where my opinion either differs slightly or where I feel further clarification is needed. Firstly, for the clarity of the record, I wish to say that I fully agree with what the two colleagues who spoke before me have said, except for the remarks I will make now. As regards the discussion about adjudicated facts and the possibility of making use of Rule 94 relating to adjudicated facts, and this issue was first raised by Madam Del Ponte, I have to say that I feel we should not take too optimistic a view of this issue because this mechanism, which is part of the ten point plan offered by the Prosecution to shorten the proceedings, it will not actually save time in practice. Why? Your Honours, in your decision, you accepted 88 adjudicated facts out of some 520, I think, presented by the Prosecution. However, in accordance with the same Rule, the Defence does have the right to challenge these facts. Out of the 88 accepted so far, I believe there are some we will have to challenge. I am saying this to show what the effect will be of taking adjudicated facts from other cases on the length of this trial. Even were the Chamber to allow a far greater number of adjudicated facts, and it seems to be what the Prosecution is seeking, it will not affect the length of the proceedings because, as my colleague Mr. Karnavas has said, the Defence will have to challenge those facts because the Defence in those cases did not have the same case, the same theory, or did not have to challenge the same facts that we have to challenge, precisely because all forms of liability are mentioned in the indictment. We have given a few examples to show why the Defence teams in those other cases perhaps did not have to challenge those facts whereas this Defence does have to challenge them. Therefore, a mechanism which at first sight might seem to have the effect of shortening the proceedings will not in fact do so in practice. Perhaps a few days may be saved, but not more. Another issue I wish to raise were the dossiers that have been discussed here. I cannot but express a general viewpoint here. The parties to these proceedings, in this case the Prosecution and the Defence, but we are referring now to something that the Prosecution has put forward, have full liberty to present their case as they wish. They can call two witnesses, 22, 302; they can present two documents, 200 documents; they can classify the documents by topic into dossiers or present the evidence in any other way they choose. It's up to the party, and in this case it's the Prosecution that is the first to present its case in these proceedings. It's up to them to decide what the best way of presenting their evidence is. Therefore, I feel that as another party to these proceedings, it's not up to me to go into this issue and to say whether the dossiers are a good thing or not. In the Kordic and Cerkez case the dossiers proved not to be a good idea. I won't go into this any further. However, dossiers also have a practical effect on the manner of work of both parties in the courtroom. Following the directive and following the assistance of the Registry, we invested a great deal of effort into preparing for e-court. We organised our work in order to be prepared for e-court. I see that some problems have emerged in this field in the meantime, and I hope they will be overcome in time. Now we are being told that if the Prosecution uses dossiers, then we as Defence might have to do the same. So now we are supposed to do something that e-court was supposed to avoid, precisely the same thing. It seems that there are at least eight and at most 12 sets of this material, and without elaborating on this, I just need to tell you that we will need at least one or two persons to deal with this. As you have heard, our resources are very limited. That is the case with Prosecution as well but they have more people than we do. Even if we had enough people on our team, all of us Defence teams in this Tribunal have to use one single photocopy machine and it is absolutely impossible for us to produce this amount of material. It is physically impossible for us. The Registry will certainly promise us that they will make everything available to us. We have had similar promises from them before, but let's be realistic: We currently do not have such resources. I don't want to go further into these details but allow me to bring one more issue to your attention. And it deals with the number of viva voce witnesses and witnesses whose written statements would be admitted into evidence. I think this affects fundamental rights of the accused to have a fair trial. I ask the Chamber to proceed extremely cautiously when deciding on these issues because the Defence has a fundamental right to challenge such evidence and that has to be taken into account, just as in case of adjudicated facts Defence teams in some other cases had no reason to challenge some issues that we have to challenge in our case. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kovacic. Mrs. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not wish to repeat what my colleagues said before me, however, I need to reiterate the following: Most of those on Defence teams who took the floor so far come from systems where the Defence is expected to assist the Prosecution and not defend their clients conscientiously and with zeal, and something that we are familiar with, those of us coming from former communist regimes. Mrs. Del Ponte called upon Defence to cooperate with the Prosecution and, in a way, make the work of Prosecution easier. This is something that we have already heard. This was deja vu for us. We think that it is utterly improper for Prosecution to expect from the Defence to give them a glimpse of their future defence and in that way assist the Prosecution and allow it to adjust its case in view of the Defence strategies. In addition to that, I think that it is also improper to have all facts mentioned in the indictment and in all of the documents considered as indisputable and then expect the Defence to state which facts in their view are going to be challenged and give their reasons for that. In addition to that, we also believe it to be improper that Defence is expected to cooperate with the Prosecution when it comes to adjudicated facts in such a way as to agree that all of these facts are beyond dispute and to limit its participation in this trial to barely just nodding to proposals of the Prosecution and to admit that the crime base presented by the Prosecution is accurate. If we are going to discuss about the ways to shorten this trial, I think that we need to start from a very thorough analysis of the indictment and see whether the Prosecution can do something about making this trial a rational one and a trial that can be conducted in a time-wise manner. If we look at all of the facts stated in relation to all of the accused in all of the charges, then we will see that all of our clients are accused of instigating, committing, aiding, abetting and there are another 15 verbs in relation to each accused. We wonder whether the Prosecution knows or has a concept of the liability in each of the accused when they are unable to state accurately what it is exactly that they are charging them with, and instead they are charging them with all theoretically known modes of liability. If we also analyse various modes of liability, we will see that even though this Tribunal permits alternative charges, we will see that there is not a single mode of liability that was not included in this indictment. This creates a huge burden for the Defence because we need to defend our clients from -- in relation to each mode of liability. We also wonder whether the Prosecution knows what are facts that they are relying on when it comes to each of our clients. This indictment includes even some outdated modes of liability. For example, aiding and abetting, joint criminal enterprise. This is something that has been ruled an improper mode of liability before this Tribunal, and it is included in this indictment. The same applies to indirect co-perpetratorship which, according to the appeal judgement in Stakic, is also impermissible, and it can be found in our indictment. If the Prosecution were to organise, both legally and factually this indictment, and if it were to turn it into an acceptable civil law indictment, then this trial would last -- would be much shorter. Another issue that I want to raise is the right to a fair trial. We discussed this in previous Status Conferences, therefore just two sentences concerning this. We believe that the political decision on the completion strategy of this Tribunal must not affect the rules concerning the trial. I'm sure that the Trial Chamber will be aware of this. One of the basic fundamental rights that all of us, including the Prosecution, need to have in mind is the right of the accused to a fair trial, and should the political decision on the length of existence of this Tribunal need to be amended, then I think that we need to get involved in this process. I think that the Judges on this Trial Chamber must be allowed to run this trial without being pressured by time limits so that they can pass a judgement which will be fair and only such a judgement can be acceptable to the victims. It is precisely because of the victims that this Tribunal was founded. Another issue that has to do with a right to fair trial, I want to say the following: According to the Rule 82(A), each of the accused has a right in a joint indictment trial to be tried as though he was the sole accused. Therefore my client, General Petkovic, is not one-sixth of the accused in this trial. No. He is an accused that has identical rights to all other accused, and I believe that this needs to be taken account when we conduct cross-examination, although we understand that relevance -- irrelevant questions should not be put, but despite of that, we think that each Defence team needs to be given an appropriate time to put questions on behalf of their client. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jonjic, you have the floor to speak about the proceedings and the duration of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I fully support what was said by my colleagues, especially Mr. Karnavas, and let me add just two or three more sentences. What I wish to say has to do with the so-called dossiers. When speaking of dossiers, we are actually discussing three, five binders pertaining to a particular event or particular area. It is true that such dossiers could be useful, both to the Chamber and Defence teams. However, I don't think that we should overestimate their use, because it is not the task of the Prosecution to establish the truth. The task of the Prosecution, as they understand it, and as rules provide, is to do everything to ensure that our clients are found guilty and sentenced accordingly. In order to achieve that task, the Prosecution will compile these dossiers in such a way as to select documents which would go to prove this. Therefore, they will do this selectively and without paying much attention to authenticity of these documents. A lot of these documents come from intelligence services, and we are aware of this based on previous trials. We know that this was done in previous trials as well. Therefore, I don't think that we should overestimate the use and value of such dossiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will be very brief. I do not want to repeat what was already stated. This plan that we received from the Prosecution really makes us doubt that this can be concluded within 450 hours. We have 16 witnesses here and the Prosecution estimates that they will need 55 to 66 -- to 60 hours for that. This means that until June the Prosecution would use about 25 per cent of the allotted time. Therefore I'm quite sceptical about whether it is realistic that the Prosecution can conclude this within 450 hours, as they estimated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before we have a break, for technical reasons, I am going to give the floor to Madam Del Ponte if she wishes to add something, but just to sum up what the Defence counsel said, they had already said what they said at the Status Conferences. There is nothing new in this respect. I only note that there are points of agreement, for example, as to the dossiers, and main points of disagreement regarding other facets. A judge is here in order to settle such issues, and this is what we are going to do as a Trial Chamber. Madam Del Ponte, do you want to have the floor before the break? MS. DEL PONTE: Just a few words, Mr. President. I shall be very brief. But I did hear things about the way we should do our work. I want to say this once and for all: That it is the Prosecutor who writes the indictment. The Defence is not here to tell us how to do it. But it is true, Mr. President, if we want to have a three-month long trial, it can be done. We just need to have an indictment with one count. But this is not a justice a la carte. This is not what I'm supposed to do. I have received my mandate from the Security Council. All the highest ranking politicians and military officers have to be tried. So I have an indictment. You have it before you. You don't like it, but that's the way it is. I have to prove what I put into the indictment because this mandate given to me by the Security Council doesn't just tell me to punish, to say choose the most serious crime. No, no. It's not what it tells me. This mandate is an overall mandate. It deals with liability. And this is what we are attempting to do here, Mr. President. This is not justice a la carte. You have the indictment as it is in front of you. We apply the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that we have, and this is merely what we are asking here and what we've been asking during the Status Conference. We said just try to apply the rules, because if you do so, you can endeavour to save time. Of course we ask the Defence for their help. Of course, with the help of the Trial Chamber, we could reduce the length of the trials. We have 92 bis, we have 89(F). These are means used or given by the rules. So don't tell me, ladies and gentlemen from the Defence teams, because look at the rule. We are not asking you, at the end of the Defence case, to tell us each and every point that the accused challenge, because this is stated in the rule. In Rule 65 ter, it said, when, when should it happen? Once the Prosecution have filed the documents mentioned in subrule (A). Or you have Rule 67, Mr. President. It does not say that it should be done after the Defence case. It says within the time limits prescribed by the Trial Chamber or by the Pre-Trial Judge. And the Pre-Trial Judge, when does he intervene? Before the trial commences. So please, Mr. President, please, Trial Chamber, Your Honours, we merely ask for the rules to be implemented, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence so as to endeavour to speed up the pace of the proceedings based on our principles. However, I also want to tell you that the Security Council will be very vigilant, despite the Resolutions, if this trial is not concluded, completed within the time limit. We are just asking the Defence to work together with us so that the trial can be conducted, of course within the respect of the fair trial principle for both parties. But I'm asking you to speed up the pace of the proceedings because it is another principle, that of an expeditious trial, that is mentioned in the rules. So I count on you, Mr. President, Your Honours, so that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence can be properly implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now ten to 4. We need to have a break, because you know that the tapes run out. The hearing shall resume in 20 minutes' time, around ten past 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are now resuming our hearing on the agenda for this Pre-Trial Conference. We mentioned that we would like to get to know the accused whom we don't know yet, so I shall now turn to the accused and ask them each in turn to introduce themselves. If you could give us your name, please. Before coming to The Hague, what position did you hold? What are you called? Because on reading the indictment I realised that some of the accused had been Prime Ministers, ministers, generals, presidents of commission, and teachers or professors, so please let me know whether you would like me to call you sir or Prime Minister or general. Please let me know. Let me remind you that you are presumed innocent until such a time that a judgement has not been rendered. You're therefore deemed to be innocent until such a time. The presumption of innocence means that you have certain rights, and you therefore are entitled to human dignity. In addition, I would like you to tell me whether you have any health problems whatsoever. I did address this issue with your lawyers at the former Status Conferences. If you have any health problems, please let me know right away because I would like to make sure that the Judges are informed about this and that we know what your health situation is in detention. I have therefore asked the Registrar to call in the doctor working in the detention unit, to send me before the 16th of May a medical certificate for each of you. All the Judges hope, of course, that you are in good health. So let me begin with the first accused, in no particular order. I would like to ask the first accused here to my right, if you could give me your title position -- name, title position, and tell me whether you have any health problems or not. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour, I am Valentin Coric. I held the following titles: Chief of police administration, minister in the Croatian government of Herceg-Bosna, minister of the interior. I was also minister of one canton within Herzegovina. I was deputy minister in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was the last post I held before coming here to The Hague. I hold the rank of major general of the Croatian Defence Council. You can address me as you wish. Now you wanted me to turn to my health. Prior to coming to The Hague in April of 2004, I had certain health problems, namely with my blood circulation system. Later on, upon my return to Zagreb, as I was waiting for the trial to commence, I was hospitalised twice. Once I had a minor stroke and then I had to do a number of blood tests. Out of six enzymes, one of them, called treponem finding from one enzyme was abnormal. The second time I was hospitalised, a very detailed blood test was done and all of the findings are normal, including the enzyme called treponem, which remains normal until this day, and I am very happy about that. I would like to use this opportunity to say something very briefly about what my former Defence counsel, Mr. Jonjic, said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will address this issue later. So it's on the agenda but we will address it at a later stage. So I would like to set this aside for the time being and come back to it later. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I hope I have answered all of your questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. THE ACCUSED PUSIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour my name is Berislav Pusic. The only position I held in the course of the war from 1993 to 2001 was the president of the Commission for Exchange of Prisoners of War and the Missing. I was involved in humanitarian work. I took part in exhumations of individual and mass graves. I cooperated with The Hague Tribunal from the initial phase of the exhumations. I was a low-ranking official and I was the only humanitarian worker who was put on trial. Even at Nuremberg none of humanitarian aid workers were tried. The last position I held was a member of the Commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina for Exchange of Persons and for De-mining. As for my health, four days after the surgery in Ljubljana, I was brought here after my voluntary surrender to The Hague Tribunal. When I released provision -- when I was released provisionally, I did not have proper medical care as I do not have medical insurance in the Republic of Croatia. I went to the Republic of Croatia against my will. I went three times to Mostar, upon receiving prior approval from the Tribunal, where I tried to undergo some medical examinations, and as you can see, my health is still quite poor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having given us these details. Mr. Ibrisimovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I think that there is a mistake in the transcript. It is stated that Mr. Pusic was president of the Exchange Commission whereas in fact he was president of the service which was involved in exchanges, and by your leave, let me say this: Judge Orie, in one of the previous Status Conferences, allowed Mr. Coric, who was trouble sitting for a long time, to get up for a minute or so every hour, if that is not disruptive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, no problem. Next person, please. Who would like to take the floor? THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon. My name is Milivoj Petkovic, I am a colonel general. I served for two terms as chief of the Main Staff of Croatian Defence Council. My last military post was chief inspection -- inspector of the Ministry of Defence of Croatia. You may address me either by "sir" or "general" as you please. I accept both. As for my health, I prepared myself, so if you say that this trial is going to last 20 years, then yes, I think that I will persevere for that long. I have some problems with my spine, with my back. I have consulted doctors and they will do everything in their power to ensure that I can carry on normally. I hope that I will be able to stay in good physical and mental health throughout. I'm sure that all assistance I need will be provided to me in the Detention Unit, as was the case during my previous five-month stay there. My father back home is quite sick. He is in terminal stage, suffering from lung cancer, and other than that, I don't have other serious family problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we know each other because we have already seen each other on other occasions but I would like you to introduce yourself, please, for those judges who don't know you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] My name is Slobodan Praljak. I'm a graduate of philosophy, sociology. I'm also a graduate engineer of electrical engineering, and I have also graduated from the academy of film and acting. I did this work before the war. During the war and aggression, I did 12 or 13 various jobs. I was assistant to Minister Gojko Susak in the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and I held a number of other posts which it would be difficult to enumerate now. By rank, I'm a colonel general of the Croatian army. I am very proud of my rank and I ask that you address me as Colonel General Slobodan Praljak. I am mentally and physically prepared to withstand everything here. Minor health problems will be solved in the Detention Unit. Whether my physical body as opposed to my metaphysical body will withstand all this is in God's hands. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED STOJIC: [Interpretation] Good day. My name is Bruno Stojic. With respect to my health, I'm quite well, at least I believe so. And as regards the conditions in the Detention Unit, I have no complaints. With respect to my previous posts, when you refer to ministers, I thought you meant me. I was a head of the Defence Ministry of the HVO, and I'm proud of this. The last position I held, seven years ago, I was director of the Dubrovnik Bank in Mostar. I have been unemployed for the last five years. I have no social security or welfare in the Republic of Croatia, but as I am now in the Detention Unit, I have been given medical checkups and my health seems to be in good order. As for the manner of addressing me, you may address me as you wish. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good day. When somebody asks me what I did, I usually say imagine a state and all the posts of that state and just add the word former in front. I was a journalist, an editor, I was a Prime Minister, I was a mayor, the mayor of Mostar before the war, the Deputy Prime Minister, and for a short time the Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina before the multi-party elections. After that, I was the managing director of a large corporation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, I held various posts. I was the Prime Minister, later on I was appointed to the transitional government in accordance with the Vance Owen Plan. After that, I was vice-president of the government, defence minister of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, minister of defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. After the Dayton Accord, I for more than five years was the minister of foreign affairs of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was reappointed several times. After that, I was in the Ministry of Trade. I served in various systems in various governments before the elections during the national party rule and then the multi-ethnic rule. I have also been university professor. I have a Ph.D. in political economy. I am in good health. This morning we were examined in the Detention Unit. I feel that I will be able to face all the challenges of this trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber through me thanks you for this introduction. Thank you for telling us in detail but very succinctly what your various positions were prior to coming to The Hague. And I note that in terms of health, even though some of you may experience some problems, generally speaking, the situation is good. Of course, don't hesitate to tell us straight away if you have a problem or refer it to the doctor in the Detention Unit or speak about it to your Defence counsel, and you can send us any mail relating to such problems if you deem it necessary. Please be aware of the fact that your personal situation will be followed up very closely and I will personally take great care to see how the situation evolves for you if you ever were to experience any problems. As you know, we are going to spend several months or even several years together in this courtroom. Needless to say, as time goes by, we will be made aware of any problem that might turn up. So the agenda of the Pre-Trial Conference calls for a major item now. The issue of Defence counsel. You know it all: The trial will commence tomorrow, officially. The Pre-Trial Conference is a hearing devoted to solving all problems prior to the commencement of trial. Luckily, for the time being, all the Defence counsel are present. There were two problems, two pending issues; one to do with Mrs. Alaburic, who wanted to choose her co-counsel. According to the latest information, she has given up her first choice. This being so, normally speaking the Registrar should appoint a co-counsel to assist Mrs. Alaburic. As I told you last time, if you were ever to fall ill or you were not available for some length of time, your client must be represented, and the lawyer must be present. So Mrs. Alaburic, do you want to say anything on this subject?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to tell you that I have not given up the idea that Mr. Orsat Miljenic should be my co-counsel. He has a great deal of experience in working with the Tribunal. To be sure in a different position, but in my view he is well acquainted with this case, both the facts and the legal issues, and in my view he would be the best possible choice for my co-counsel. I have discussed this with General Petkovic, and I would like him to express his opinion also in connection with Mr. Miljenic and all the issues that have arisen. What I have changed my mind about is the following: The proposal that Mr. Orsat Miljenic be appointed pursuant to Rule 44 is something I have replaced with notice that we have appointed him -- I apologise. The first rule I wish to mention is Rule 45, but instead of this, I now wish to say that we have appointed him pursuant to Rule 44 and that he will do this work pro bono until the summer break by which time we hope to find a more permanent solution, either with Mr. Orsat Miljenic or without him, with counsel who is on list 45. In this way, we have resolved one part of the issue I addressed the Chamber about, and this has to do with the experience an attorney has to have in order to be appointed counsel or co-counsel in line with Rule 45. The remaining issues have to do with interests. It seems to me that the Prosecution has not submitted any submissions. We just have the general opinion that someone who worked in the Croatian Office for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, in a manner of speaking, some way participated in the work of the OTP and this would prevent my colleague from being appointed co-counsel. General Petkovic is fully acquainted with all the former posts held by Mr. Orsat Miljenic, and General Petkovic and I decided together that I should propose to my colleague that he join the attorneys office and we started collaborating two years ago. I won't repeat what I have stated in my submissions. If the Prosecution wishes to further expand on its arguments in connection with conflict of interest, I would be very pleased to hear their arguments. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall give the floor to General Petkovic on this issue, but before I do so, let me make the following remark: You said that under Rule 44, you decided to suggest this lawyer to the Registrar, but this means that, as Rule 44 states, this lawyer is paid by your client. If your client has the financial means to pay him, the issue of you being assigned counsel arises under Rule 45. So how do you solve that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stated right away that my colleague Orsat Miljenic will do the work of co-counsel in this team pro bono, which means free of charge. My client, General Petkovic, is duty-bound, pursuant to the Registrar's decision, to participate in paying his part of his Defence to the amount of $180.000. However, he's unable to pay this amount. The bank accounts of my colleague Orsat Miljenic can be checked and it will be easy to see that he will not earn a single dollar or euro by working on this case. So it is clear he will be working pro bono or free of charge. My team has looked into the jurisprudence and we found a similar case before the Tribunal in Rwanda. Unfortunately, I have not prepared to discuss this issue at great detail so I have not noted down the name of the case, however, I can check it during the break, and a decision was reached in that case which I propose here; that is that the lead counsel is funded by the Tribunal and the co-counsel is working pro bono. Therefore, I am not proposing something that would constitute a precedent. It is something that has already happened before an International Tribunal. In my view, this would be a fair solution because my client would have a co-counsel that he accepts as appropriate, I would be working with a -- my colleague with whom I have been working for the past two years, and I believe that in this way we will enable the proceedings to go on without hindrance. If the Registrar were to choose my co-counsel, we would be having a person entering the proceedings at this stage who knows nothing of the case and who would not be able to stand in for me. With my colleague as my co-counsel, he would be able indeed to stand in for me and this would be a fair solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your co-counsel would be working pro bono. One issue remains, that of the conflict of interest, because the said co-counsel would have already worked for the Office of the Prosecutor. But I have some very obvious examples that show that individuals having worked for the Office of the Prosecutor became Defence counsel in various cases. So the notion of conflict of interests is a very flexible one, as it were. General Petkovic, what can you say on this? Because you are the first one to be involved in this. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have discussed this at length with my counsel and I feel we have found the best possible solution, or rather, the one that is best for me. At least, that's what I think and I think that this should be taken into account. I do not speak another language and I would need an interpreter to talk to another co-counsel. As for Orsat Miljenic, I know what posts he held and I am sure that this will not affect my situation in any way. Therefore, in order for the proceedings to continue without obstruction, I kindly ask Your Honours to accept the solution proposed by my counsel. I would have a co-counsel I can rely upon who is familiar with the case. If I were to have a co-counsel who is not familiar with the case, one I cannot communicate with, that is somebody I do not actually need. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Second item relating to Defence counsel, and I now turn to Mr. Coric. First let me -- before I give the floor to Mr. Coric, let me ask his counsel whether he wants to discuss this in private session or not. If he does, we will move into private session. If he feels that we can talk about this in open session, we will do so. So what do you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no objection to this discussion being held in open session. I have nothing to hide. But let me say the following: The fact that a confidential ex parte submission was handed round to all parties, including the Prosecution, and that at the last session we discussed something that was confidential and ex parte has made it possible for the Prosecution to gain insight into the weaknesses of a Defence team. However, they have not expressed any gratitude for this. If, however, the Tribunal feels or the Bench feels that we can raise this issue in public session, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's mention this in open session. The issue of a Defence counsel is a fundamental one, indeed. The accused must be assisted by counsel. So far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Majority decision of the Trial Chamber has been made. We are going to move into private session. Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have to speed things up a little bit because we have only one hour left. We will have to finish in an hour's time. We shall render this decision in writing, having to do with the guidelines that are designed to prepare for an appropriate management of this trial. I would like to address the issue of the guidelines designed to help this Court, this trial unfold as best as possible. In March 2006 I had rendered a decision and filings had been made by both parties. We had had an opportunity to discuss this on several occasions. At our last Status Conference on the 12th of April 2006, the Prosecution presented a ten point outline, the purpose of which was to cut down on the Prosecution case. The Trial Chamber has scrutinised the proposal put forward by the Prosecution, as well as by all the proposals put forward by Defence counsel, would like to make this trial as short as possible. In order to achieve this, the Trial Chamber notes as follows: The length of the Prosecution case will be limited to one year. The Trial Chamber has taken into account the fact that that equals 46 weeks or 920 hours, if you do away with the six weeks' recess overall and various UN holidays. Therefore, according to this decision, which will be handed over to you in writing tomorrow, the Trial Chamber, after having conferred, rules that the Prosecution will have 400 hours for the -- their examination-in-chief, and the -- of their witnesses. This calculation does not bear in mind the time needed by Defence counsel for their cross-examination, does not bear in mind procedural issues nor questions put by the Bench either. At this stage, the Trial Chamber does not intend to limit the time of the cross-examination of Defence counsel. The Trial Chamber has based its calculation on the fact that Defence counsel will jointly - and I would like to underline the word "jointly" - the same time as the Prosecution -- will have the same time as the Prosecution, and the time given to the Defence should be shared between the various Defence counsel of the co-accused. The Trial Chamber will stringently monitor use of time, and if need be, the Trial Chamber will take any additional decision according to circumstances and difficulties encountered. The Bench has felt that this was a good working plan. The decision could be amended at a later stage, of course, but you know from experience when Defence counsel will take the floor, you will not all repeat the same thing. Therefore, this is a good way of using our time. As far as adducing evidence is concerned, this is a very important point, so please pay attention. As a rule, the exhibits will be filed via each witness. The Trial Chamber will in due course look into the question of written statements according to Rules 92 bis and 89(F) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. As far as admission of exhibits via expert witnesses are concerned, as a rule, the Trial Chamber does not intend -- the Trial Chamber only wishes to tender the report and those points which have been discussed in the presence of the witness when he is called -- he or she is called to testify. The Trial Chamber will not accept to tender all the documents mentioned in the expert report. Let me give you an example. If, for instance, 400 exhibits are mentioned in a given report, if the expert witness will only talk about 20 or 30 of the exhibits, those 30 exhibits will be tendered into evidence but the remaining 370 will not be tendered into evidence. In the event that the Defence -- but this also applies to the Prosecution when the time comes. In the event that a party disputes the authenticity of an exhibit, a reasoned objection will have to be filed. I'm speaking about the authenticity of an exhibit, I'm not talking about reliability, which is a different issue. The Trial Chamber accepts evidence in the form of a dossier. However, this is now a very important question. Presentation of a case in the form of a dossier does not mean that the party that presents the dossier does not have to comply with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. That still applies. Which means, in other words -- let me refer to the Gornji Vakuf dossier which you have all been able to read. The Gornji Vakuf dossier contains five volumes. Certain files contain maps and lists of people's names, and in the second part you will find witness statements. The Prosecution must provide us with a dossier without the exhibits, to begin with, at any rate. The dossier comprises a number of items; maps, witness lists, and various number of other items, but no exhibits. The exhibits will only be included in the dossier once the witness has had an opportunity to discuss it and has been cross-examined. After that, at a second stage, these exhibits will be included in the dossier. The Prosecution, if it so wishes, can then ask the Trial Chamber to be given a number for the particular dossier, which means that, as far as Gornji Vakuf is concerned, we will have a small dossier containing maps, lists of witness lists, paragraphs of the indictment, reference to paragraphs in the pre-trial brief, and then afterwards, when witnesses come to talk about Gornji Vakuf, the exhibits can then be added on to this dossier. I hope Mr. Mundis has understood all of this, but this will be spelled out in our written decision. This was done because all and everyone felt that a dossier was a useful instrument but it was also designed to protect the rights of the accused. From a personal standpoint, and I shall not quote any witness names, but I have realised that the Prosecution, according to what I had asked, the Prosecution has cross-referenced the exhibits with a number of witnesses, so you have all received a CD-ROM. I've had this CD-ROM printed out, and I'm sure you have the same, and if you look at this, you will be able to realise that we have a number of exhibits and a number of witnesses. Number of exhibits that are likely to be presented to the witnesses total 320. Mr. Mundis will certainly encounter a problem here. How, when a witness is in the witness box, how will you be able to adduce 320 exhibits? You will have to, as one of the Defence counsel has stated, you will have to make a selection and adduce those exhibits that are relevant. There is no point in drowning all and everyone in too large a number of exhibits. As I have said, there are 320 exhibits. This is in the CD-ROM which you have been provided with. The Prosecution must think about this. Also I had drawn the attention of all the parties, people present, but Mr. Karnavas also mentioned this a while ago: We should not overlook the fact that when an exhibit is presented to a witness, the questions put either by the Prosecution or by the Defence can concern one or other paragraph of the said document but when the Judges of the Bench need to deliberate on the probative value and relevance of the exhibits, we may be more interested in some of the paragraphs which haven't been mentioned here. As Defence counsel, when the time comes for the cross-examination, maybe it is more important for you to consider those elements which you deem to be the most important. It is important not to overlook this. When we need to compare this exhibit with other exhibits, when we render our judgement, we can mention parts of the document which will not have been mentioned here because, when an exhibit is being admitted into evidence, it is the entire exhibit and not just one paragraph. This also applies to you, when you will be calling your witnesses to testify, and presenting -- and when you will be presenting your exhibits. I'm sure you will have thousands of exhibits. The same applies to you; you will be asking a number of questions on a particular document but the Judges will look at the entire document. Be aware of the fact that judges will read everything. I say "everything" [In English] All. [Interpretation] Furthermore, regarding the filing of Defence submissions, the Trial Chamber encourages the Defence, as much as is possible, of course, to file motions and replies jointly. Situations may arise where you all agree, so there is no need for six submissions or six replies to say one and the same thing. So it's up to you to share the work load with the six Defence teams signing one and the same motion. However, if you do not agree, of course you are free to file motions yourselves. This is just an encouragement to you from the Chamber. When a motion is filed by either party, as a rule, the Trial Chamber will not allow any reply. So you file your motion, you have a first reply by the other party, and that's it. We are not going to play table tennis here, legal table tennis. Regarding the e-court system, you all know that we are going to use this e-court system during the trial. However, the Trial Chamber would like, when a witness is called to testify, and when a party submits documents to the witness, that the party presenting the documents supply the Trial Chamber with the hard copies of the documents. I'm not asking you to make 25 photocopies. If there is one photocopy, that's enough. Four is even better. And the judges will be grateful for this. But given the means you have available, you may not be able to do more than one photocopy. Personally speaking, I have experienced one trial already in which this was not an issue. I don't see why it should be an issue in this trial. The chart, witness list and exhibit list.
