Further to the order of the 30th of November 2005, the Prosecution submitted to the Trial Chamber this famous chart. However, I'm looking at you, Mr. Mundis. I can see that what has been done is not quite complete, given what I had asked you to do. The missing link or part is the reference to the liability of each and every accused under 7(1) or 7(3). If you had done so, the Judges would have been able to understand the way you articulate your case better and the Defence would have been better able to prepare for cross-examination. You're going to tell me that you were under time pressure, et cetera, so in the future, I do urge you, when you provide us with the next chart, to endeavour to put across each witness the nature of the allegation. Does it concern all of them, all of the six, or only four or only one? Only you know this. I also remind you that the charts must be filed on a regular basis. Here, this chart takes us to July. But after July, every three weeks we must be provided with a chart for the next two weeks, with regard to witnesses. This is doable. You know that, Mr. Mundis. And this would apply to the Defence as well. You must understand that whatever I say to Mr. Mundis I am saying to you as well, Defence counsel. Regarding Mr. Donia, expert witness Donia, under 94 bis, as you know, several accused challenged his quality of expert. The Trial Chamber noted that this witness testified as an expert in many cases; therefore deems him an expert, but it is up to the Defence counsel to challenge his expert quality. Mr. Donia will come to the stand and you will be free during cross-examination to challenge everything about him. Testimony of expert witness William Tomljanovich. Mr. Mundis, according to your submissions, I understood that Mr. Tomljanovich, or Tomzanovic [phoen], will testify on the 13th, 14th and 15th of June; very soon, therefore. Today, we still have not received his expert report. I think the Defence teams may not have received it either. So Mr. Mundis, make sure you produce the report by the 12th of May. Make sure that the Defence teams, who will have two weeks under Rule 94 bis, file their remarks. Regarding pending motions, a decision will be issued soon under Rule 70, but this should not be a problem. This is going to be done very soon. Under Rule 94 bis, Mr. Praljak had asked for leave to testify or to make a statement. He is so granted by the Trial Chamber. This regards his opening statement. At this stage, Mr. Mundis, do you -- how much time do you need for your opening statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution -- as Mr. Scott indicated previously, the Prosecution anticipates that it will take no more than one full court day. There could be a little bit of slippage there; in other words, it might go slightly longer than that, but we fully expect that we can do it in one full court day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We discussed this among Judges. If you need the full court day tomorrow, Mr. Praljak will have all of Thursday. If, unfortunately, there is some slippage and you need some time on Thursday, we will have to have a morning hearing. I do urge you to limit yourself to Wednesday for your opening statement. So to keep things equal, Mr. Praljak will have all of Thursday. So Wednesday we'll have the Prosecution and Mr. Praljak will have the Thursday. But mind this: Mr. Praljak's lawyer or Mr. Praljak himself will have to tell us if they need somebody's help because it is planned to have visual aids, slides, or something, I'm not quite sure. So can we have some specifications as to the way to run this? Mr. Praljak, could you shed some light on your plans on Thursday, without really speaking on the merits, of course. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, technically everything has been prepared. It's on the computer. We have the whole presentation ready. The person who will be providing technical assistance to me is already here, becoming familiar with the Court procedure. I think that this will be expeditious and exciting, not boring, in all aspects. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the event that we have video footage or maps or charts, flow charts, I ask the Registry, and it has not been denied so far, I've asked for a large screen to be displayed in the courtroom so that the screen can be positioned above the witness's seat so as to make it possible for the Trial Chamber, the accused, and the parties to see it. Of course, the public in the public gallery should also have a large screen. It will be easier to have a large display to see what is in a document rather than on this monitor which is big enough as it is, but sometimes if you have a large screen, you see better. I'm looking at Mr. Frejabue, our court deputy. The Registry has committed itself to preparing this. I hope everything will be available very soon. I don't know how they are going to do it, but there could be a video projector, that's quite possible and feasible. Everybody will be able to see much more easily. We still have 20 minutes left. I'm now turning to the Prosecution. Mr. Mundis, do you want to intervene? But let's move just for a few minutes to private session, to tackle another subject. Please, Mr. Court deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now turning to Mr. Mundis in open session. Do you have anything to mention to the Trial Chamber? The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. We note, Mr. President, that the Trial Chamber has rendered a decision concerning the issues concerning counsel. We did, with respect to one of those issues, wish to file something and we will be doing so tomorrow, notwithstanding the Trial Chamber's earlier decision as announced at the beginning of this session. That's really the only outstanding issue that we have arising from today's conference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. I can see that Mr. Karnavas is eager to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am. Mr. President, Your Honours, I know it's late in the day. I have to register my disappointment -- I know you don't like hearing that, Mr. President, but disappointment it is with your announcement that we will jointly have to share the time on cross-examination. Just briefly, if I could just give an example. If, for instance, Mr. Donia were to testify for two hours, that would be 120 minutes. If you divide that by six, then that doesn't leave much for any particular counsel to do anything, if at all. And when you look at what Donia has done in six prior cases - and I've read all his transcripts - he alone, as I indicated last time, is about a three- or four-day cross-examination, and I say that because, when you look at his report, you don't see any footnotes and the footnotes that you do see are from newspaper articles. So in order to challenge this individual -- and I'm not saying that he's not an expert in the sense that he's got a Ph.D. in a particular area for a particular period of time, but for what he has been called to do in this case and in other cases, I dare say it's gone a little bit beyond his expertise, and so in any event, I'm registering my disappointment, and also I'm hoping that the Court or the -- Your Honours will be a little bit more flexible because we aren't -- I understand that there is this concept of joint criminal enterprise. When we are treated as jointly, then it only feeds into this mindset that there is such a thing, that we get together and then we jointly sort of figure out what we are going to be doing, and that's not the case, which is probably why on many occasions we don't join each other's motions or we don't file joint motions. That's one. Number 2, disclosure. Disclosure is still coming in. There are some unresolved issues. I can speak with Mr. Mundis privately, I don't need to take the time right now, but at some point I think it would be -- it would really help us if the Trial Chamber were to put a deadline, say, for instance, as of August 1, no more disclosure in the case, this is it, forget it. If you come up with some other witnesses, they cannot be introduced. Now, I understand in the system it's very difficult to do that, but they've had eight years. On the other hand, if we are going to have a short trial, if the case continues to grow, how can we possibly live within a time limit? So I would urge the Trial Chamber to consider that, and I'm begging the Prosecution to be a little more forthcoming with some of the disclosure that they anticipate having, and perhaps at some point they can address the Trial Chamber as to what remains out there, what they think remains out there. And I'm not referring to where they have to react based on what comes out in court. Obviously they have an obligation to do that. But certainly they shouldn't be going out there trying to develop new leads that they haven't explored already. Witness lists. You know, here we are, on the eve of trial, I have a list of some witnesses up until June. They have 185, according to Madam Del Ponte. Why can't I have the order of the witness list, and why can't we have all of this done by now? You've indicated that they haven't met fully your expectations with respect to the proofing chart. I understand they are labouring in a hard -- but they've had five months. We've got some of it, not all of it, and I think we are going to need to do a little bit better. I think you're a little bit overly generous with them, Mr. President, if I may say so. I would probably be a little tougher, but I've never been a judge, so you know. But I think -- you have to understand that the trial days are very difficult for us and we don't have enough time to react to everything. We don't have the resources. So if I'm just getting a list for two weeks, in advance, it's very difficult for me to deal with motions, look into all this other material, check and see what else is out there. Which brings me to my next point. This fellow, Tomljanovich, he was an employee of the Office of the Prosecution -- he's still, thank you. And it begs the question: How on earth we don't have a report yet? What's he doing? Is this -- is he writing -- what is going to produce? I need to react. I need to check it. How can I do that, prepare for court, and now you're giving me this Herculean task. You're saying to me be efficient in court, and as I indicated last time, for me to be efficient, I need to spend more time preparing. If I'm getting that report two weeks -- and I only have two weeks to react to it in front of everything else, it's a little bit -- I think, Mr. President, Your Honours, you should ask for their -- his report by the end of the weekend, and let Mr. Tomljanovich come here and he can give us explanation why he hasn't provided his pay masters with that report. And if he can't produce, he should get fired. It's as simple as that. I'm a little bit worried, as I said, about Mr. Donia. I think if the Prosecution ends up putting him on for two hours, there is no way on Earth that I alone, let alone all six of us, could cross-examine him for two hours. It is physically impossible and I think it would be a miscarriage of justice to hold us to that. As I indicated, I'm prepared to try to provide with a list of all the questions I would have asked if I had the opportunity. I don't want to go that route, but I do think, at least as we start with some of these very, very important witnesses, because they are bringing in the big guns early on, as you can see, they are not bringing in some crime-base witnesses. These are heavy hitters that take a lot of time to prepare, and I think as we start, at least, I beg for your consideration for a little bit more time. One other issue before I get to a technical issue. My client would like to have the use of a computer in court. He's computer literate, has been forever, and I think it's important for him to have those resources. He's entitled to assist in his own defence, he wishes to assist in his own defence, and in that vein I also wish to emphasise that I made a request that he be provided or he be allowed to use the internet while he's in the facilities. And I say this not because he's going to be or should be communicating privately or doing private affairs but everything that we have is electronic. You have this electronic disclosure system. You have the JDB. He should be entitled to do his own research, and it would also be important for him to communicate with me, if need be. So that's a technical issue that we need to at least think about. I've asked the Registry to think about it. I'm not being dogmatic, neither is my client, but nonetheless I want to press as much as I can. We are in the age of technology and we can't say, well, gee, they may disclose something while they were out on provisional release. And nobody raised that issue, that they shouldn't have the use of the internet. Why, all of a sudden, now they are going to be a threat where they are under the watchful guise [sic] of the United Nations here in The Hague. Lastly, one minor technical issue. My client informed me that on page 35, line 24, apparently he had indicated one of his positions which was misinterpreted. Perhaps, rather than me saying what he said, perhaps he can be given the opportunity to correct the record so I don't get it wrong. And again I apologise, I don't mean to be disrespectful when I say I'm disappointed, but on the other hand, I have to raise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic, did you want to correct something in the transcript? THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Microphone not activated] transcript, but I saw just after finish my remarks that it was [B/C/S spoken]. So I said president of executive council of Mostar, which means president of government. Prime Minister is not the same as president of government. Second, I mentioned during war that I was president of temporary executive council of Croatian community Herceg-Bosna, and later on Prime Minister -- president of government of Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. The first part wasn't translated at all. And at the end, I said that I had Ph.D., if I'm able to recall, in international economy. It was said just political economy. So I said international relations -- international economy and political economy. So I think that those three issues should be changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It will be done so. The transcript will be corrected. Mrs. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, during the trainings organised by our Bar association for counsel who are new, on such cases we were told that sometimes, and maybe even often, we will be saying things not for any other purpose but to put them on the record. I hope that this will not be said of my next remark which has to do with the amount of time allotted for cross-examination. I fully agree with Mr. Karnavas, and I wish to add the following: Namely, that this violates the principle of equality of arms in this trial. The Prosecution not only has the time for examination-in-chief, but they also have on their side additional material, evidence, documents that they want to introduce through that witness. So we cannot speak of any equality of arms if we are only analysing the allotted time and not the entire documentation. My other remark means -- is that the rights of each accused will be adversely affected if each of them is given only one-sixth of the time allotted to the Prosecution. This goes contrary to Rule 82(A). The Defence of Mr. Petkovic will appeal this decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor, I wanted to respond to Mr. Karnavas. Regarding the issue of the computer or the laptop, Mr. Frejabue, please check with your Registry to see whether it's possible for accused to have laptops during the hearing. It's not up to me, it's up to the Registry. I went to the Tribunal web site no later than this afternoon. 36 computers were given to Bosnia-Herzegovina. They went off in a truck. So maybe laptops can be made available to the accused. Regarding your disappointment, please trust the Trial Chamber. Don't be overly disappointed. Of course, the issue of the expert witness which you challenge, why can't you, all of you six Defence teams, decide as to the one who is going to cross-examine in chief as it were? You don't need all of you to repeat the same questions again and again. So just agree among yourselves, because when it comes to the historic factors, there should be some consensus among the Defence if they want to challenge specific facts mentioned in the so-called expert report. So I think you could agree among yourselves. Also don't forget that the -- you yourselves will have an opportunity to call your own experts. Do not forget that. This is now the Prosecution case but you will have your Defence case, during which you will be free to call whomever you want. I mean, fair trial, it's a fair trial between the two parties, right? Balanced between the two parties. We'll see how all of this unfolds but very soon you'll realise that questions have been already put by a colleague of yours so there is no need to repeat it, but of course, the Trial Chamber will listen to you if you want to take the floor, which is now the case. So I do give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I must confess that it seems to me that in the ruling of the Trial Chamber about expert witnesses, you resolved this dilemma. If I misunderstood you, you can correct me, but it seems you have resolved this dilemma concerning the expert witness by saying that only what they state viva voce will be admitted into evidence. I'm saying this not because I'm trying to amend your ruling but let me say that our greatest problem is that such rulings are strictly applied only initially and later on the application becomes more loose. When it comes to expert witnesses which will be testifying against all of the accused, we would like to kindly ask you to be somewhat more lenient when it comes to time in those cases. Naturally, all of the Defence teams will try to do as you instructed us; namely, to divide the time among us, and we hope that none of those questions will be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Back to the issue of the expert witnesses, the accused were not present last time and I think it needs to be stated again. Donia is an expert witness who testified on several occasions in various trials. I looked at the Blaskic judgement, at the Kordic judgement, and if I remember well, in the Blaskic judgement, this is a witness who testified for days on end. Well, in the Blaskic judgement, there are two footnotes. Two. In Kordic, unless I'm mistaken, there are three of them. So that's the problem as it stands. Do we have to devote entire hours to arrive at a situation where -- when judges, after 15 days of testimony, only use two words, two footnotes with referral to a footnote? This is food for thought. Regarding the other expert, I'm hearing this for the first time, he's an employed person with the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Mundis, you should give this report to the Defence very soon. Why should they be left without it, especially if the report is 50, 100 or 200 pages long? They need time to look into it, to scrutinise it, and to pass it on to the accused who may also have relevant remarks to make. We just have a few minutes left. Yes, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly, I think an issue raised by the Defence of Mr. Praljak and Mr. Kovacic remains. I think Mr. Karnavas also spoke about it. It concerns the right of the accused to put questions in exceptional circumstances. I believe that this has to do with expert witnesses. We have not heard what the position of the Chamber is in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For the time being, we have not discussed -- or the Bench has not discussed this issue yet. I have told you what my personal point of view is but I don't know if the other Judges share my point of view. Personally, I feel that I have no objections to Mr. Praljak completing the question or supplementing the questions put by his Defence counsel, but the Judges of the Bench need to agree with this. This is something we are going to look into and we will let you know what our position is. We still have a few days ahead of us and we shall inform you of our position. Mr. Kovacic, you're remaining very silent. Would you like to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add, my colleague has interpreted this previous discussion more or less correctly. I believe it was an oral motion made by my client while he was representing himself. I feel that there are other witnesses where it would be very useful and practical for the accused to put questions directly. I will now invent a scenario. Let's say you and I were in the same place a few years ago and you're talking about this to a third person and you remember a certain beech tree that was there, and it jogs your memory. So it's useful to put questions of this kind. The witness might say to me, I don't remember, but when he looks my client in the eye, he couldn't say that. It might be useful to jog the memory of witnesses. Your Honour, if I may add very briefly in connection with examination of expert witness Donia, Your Honour stated very correctly that in the Blaskic and Kordic judgements, he is mentioned in only a few footnotes. Let me remind you, however, that these footnotes represent the basis for further conclusions made by the Chamber in those cases. I agree with what Your Honours say, that so much time was spent in those cases on this one expert witness but the results were minimal. Let me remind you, however, that the Defence of the accused Prlic proposed that this testimony, or rather, this witness be not called at all. If we look at this from the standpoint efficacy and expeditiousness, regardless of the time frame set by Your Honours, I am convinced that because of the relevance of the questions put by the Defence, you will extend our time. I'm certain of it, because Your Honours will see that the questions truly are relevant. We will lose a lot of time with Donia and the result will be precisely what Your Honours have stated. It is an irrelevant testimony and we should not waste time on it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a few minutes left. Let me turn to the accused. Would one of the accused like to say something? Mr. Praljak raised his hand. Could you be brief, please, because the interpreters from now on are working overtime. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I will be brief. I wish to leave open the possibility in the case of certain witnesses, especially those we call experts, a historian however cannot be an expert, he can only provide the Court with information, because if you take ten historians, they will mutually disagree. All he can do is bring documents. But his opinion is relevant only as information, not as an expert. An expert may be a surgeon, a ballistic expert, or another kind of scientist in the exact sciences, so I ask Your Honours for leave to question these so-called experts myself, because my own knowledge is so much greater than theirs that I will be able to expose them. THE ACCUSED PUSIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. There is an old adage that whoever does something makes mistakes. I believe that the Prosecution has made a big mistake in raising the indictment and they have chosen the wrong person for this. In the war which is behind us, many people called Pusic played a role. The Prosecution still has time to withdraw the indictment in my case. Thank you. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I will be very brief. I support this motion that we the accused should have the right to put questions to witnesses. I especially wish to draw attention to my own situation and I wish to assist my future counsel by putting a question now and then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do other people wish to say something? No. In that case, Mr. Mundis, just in a few seconds because the Prosecution would always -- would like to be the last to speak. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, I will be very brief. On the issue of whether the accused are permitted or offered an opportunity to question witnesses, the Prosecution certainly would like to be heard on that particular issue prior to the Trial Chamber rendering a decision allowing that. We believe that an informed decision is one in which all of the parties have a right to be heard and we would ask for an opportunity to fully brief that issue and to fully set forth the Prosecution's view on that. We've alluded to this in one of our earlier filings, and we simply at this point would take the view, Your Honours, that although the accused have an absolute right to remain silent, that at any point when they exercise any rights to speak, including questioning witnesses, that anything that they say, the way they formulate a question, any hypothesis that's built into the question, can certainly be construed as a statement which we will seek to use against them at any opportunity that we can do so. And that would be our position in a nutshell. We would like the opportunity to more fully brief that issue prior to the Trial Chamber rendering a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you would like to file submissions, you have all night to draft these. You can file your submissions as of tomorrow morning onwards. As Mr. Karnavas said, you have a armada standing behind you, so make use of the armada and file your submissions. We the Judges -- well, I'm sure -- I believe that behind the wall there are a number of people sitting there, and we will have to rule on this. It is now ten minutes past 7. I apologise to the interpreters. As you know, we shall reconvene tomorrow at quarter past 2, and we will have our hearing until 7 p.m. and we shall reconvene again on Thursday. Thank you, and see you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
